en: Petavatthu, Ubbarivagga, 9. The Story of Aṅkura’s Ghost [The Blessed One said: "Monks, in the past, in a certain village, there was a householder named Aṅkura. He was wealthy, possessed of great riches, with abundant grain-stores, and owner of many gold coins, bullion, and treasures. He had a wife who was beautiful, fair to behold, and charming; she was well-versed in song, dance, and instrumental music. Then, monks, the householder Aṅkura, having taken his meal, sat down on a high seat. His wife, having adorned herself with all her finery, approached him. Having approached, she stood behind the householder Aṅkura, fanning him. Then, monks, the householder Aṅkura, overcome by passion for his wife, spoke thus to her: 'Come, my dear, let us enjoy ourselves. 'Wait, master! My mother-in-law is sitting right here. Wait until she has gone away. 'Come, my dear, let us enjoy ourselves now! 'Wait, master! My father-in-law is sitting right here. Wait until he has gone away. 'Come, my dear, let us enjoy ourselves now! 'Wait, master! My husband's younger brother is sitting right here. Wait until he has gone away. 'Come, my dear, let us enjoy ourselves now! 'Wait, master! My husband's elder brother is sitting right here.

“For whose sake we go to Kamboja as carriers of wealth—
this yakkha is the giver of desires.”
We lead this yakkha away; having seized this yakkha,
we shall subdue him by force with our strength.
"Having mounted the vehicle,
let us go quickly to Dvāraka.
"In the shade of whichever tree..."
One may sit or lie down [there],
but one should not break its branch;
for a betrayer of friends is an evil person.
“One might even cut off the trunk of that tree in whose shade one has sat or slept.”
“If the purpose were such that one might sit or lie down in the shade of a tree— ”
One should not break its fruit,
for a treacherous friend is evil.
“Of whatever tree one sits in the shade, [one should not cut it down].”
One may sit or lie down;
one should uproot that [defilement] entirely,
if such were the purpose.
“One should not think even in one’s mind of evil toward that person in whose house one might dwell for even a single night and where one receives food and drink.”
Gratitude is praised by the virtuous.
Even for one who has stayed in another's house for but a single night,
provided with food and drink;
One should not even think of evil toward him with the mind;
for one whose hands are innocent does not burn the betrayer of friends who previously performed good deeds.
For later one is harmed by evil;
a person slain by his own speech does not see what is auspicious.
“Neither by god nor by human,
nor by power am I easily overcome;
I am a yakkha who has attained supreme psychic power.”
“Far-reaching, endowed with beauty and strength.
“The color of your hand is entirely beautiful;
it is a fivefold flow of honey-sweet nectar.”
"Various flavors drip forth;
I think you are Purindada.
"I am neither a deva nor a gandhabba," [he replied].
Nor even Sakka Purindada;
know me, Aṅkura, as a peta who has come here from Roruva.
“What was your character and what was your conduct in the city of Roruva?
By what holy life did you [attain this]?”
“Merit succeeds in the hand.
“In the past I was a weaver;
at that time I was in Roruva.”
My livelihood was difficult and I was poor;
I had nothing to give.
I possessed only a dwelling.
In the vicinity of Asayha—
of the faithful master of giving,
who has performed meritorious deeds and possesses a sense of shame.
Therein, "to the beggars" refers to mendicants of various clans;
they questioned me there.
The dwelling of Asayha.
Where shall we go, may you be blessed?
Where is alms being given?
Being questioned by them, I declare the abode of the Unconquerable,
having raised my right arm.
Go there, may it be well with you;
there alms are given at the abode of Asayha.
By that hand it was the giver of desires,
by that hand it was the source of honeyed sweetness;
by that same holy life of mine—
“Merit succeeds in the hand.
“It seems you have not given a gift to anyone with your own hands;”
Rejoicing in another’s gift,
he raised his hand and spoke; by that hand,
he became a granter of desires.
Therefore, there is a honey-sweetness in his hand;
through that holy life,
merit succeeds in his hand.
He who, O Bhante, gave gifts with his own hands out of faith—
having abandoned this human body—
"Has he indeed gone to the state of the Seers?
"I do not know the going or the coming of the Aṅgīrasa, who has overcome what is difficult to overcome."
"I have heard from Vessavaṇa that Asayha has gone to the companionship of Sakka.
"It is indeed enough to do what is wholesome."
Seeing the hand that grants all desires, who would not perform meritorious deeds in order to give gifts as is fitting?
Truly, having gone from here and reached Dvārakā,
I shall establish a distribution of gifts.
Whatever would bring me happiness—
I shall give food and drink,
as well as clothing and lodgings.
“The mirage, the well,
and the narrow passages on difficult paths.
“By whom were your fingers made crooked?”
Your face is contorted and your eyes are streaming;
what evil deed have you committed?
“Of the householder Aṅgīrasa,
the seeker of the home of faith;
in his distribution of gifts, I— ”
I was preeminent in giving.
There, upon seeing supplicants who had arrived seeking food, I would act.
Stepping aside to one side,
I made my mouth into a funnel;
by that means, my fingers became crooked.
My mouth is distorted,
and my eyes are streaming;
that evil deed was committed by me.
“By this act of yours, O base man,
your mouth has been distorted,
and your eyes are streaming with tears.”
Because he made his mouth like a funnel for another’s gift—
how indeed could one giving a gift [be otherwise]?
One should provide for another’s benefit:
food, drink, hard food,
as well as clothing and lodgings.
"Indeed, having gone from here and reached Dvārakā,
I shall establish a distribution of gifts."
Whatever may bring me happiness—
food and drink, as well as clothing and lodgings— I shall give them.
“The mirage, the well,
and the narrow mountain passes”—
having turned back from there, he...
Having arrived at the gateway,
Aṅkura established a gift that brought him happiness.
He gave food and drink,
as well as clothing and lodgings,
and a well with an abundance of water.
With a serene mind:
"Who is hungry? Who is thirsty?
Who shall put on a garment?"
Whose yokes are ready? Let them harness the vehicle from here.
Who desires a parasol and perfume?
"Who [wants] a garland?
Who [wants] sandals?"— thus did the barbers and cooks of Magadha proclaim there.
Always, both evening and morning,
at Aṅkura’s dwelling:
“Aṅkura sleeps happily,” [they said].
Thus people know me:
"Sindhaka sleeps in suffering because he does not see any supplicants."
"The sprout sleeps happily," so people know of me;
"Sindhaka, I sleep in suffering."
“Even if there were only a few forest-dwellers.
“If Sakka, the lord of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, were to grant you a boon;”
“Of all this world,
what boon do you wish to choose as the best?
“If Sakka were to grant me a boon,” [he replied].
The Lord of the Thirty-three,
while I was still rising from my bed,
appeared at the time of sunrise.
May divine foods appear,
and may virtuous ones come as supplicants;
may my giving never be exhausted.
Having given, may I have no regret;
while giving, may I gladden my heart—
this, Sakka, is the boon I choose.”
“One should not bestow all of one’s wealth upon others;
one should give gifts while also protecting one’s property.
Therefore, indeed, wealth itself is better than giving.”
Through excessive giving, families are ruined.
The wise do not praise neither non-giving nor excessive giving.
"Therefore, indeed, wealth alone is better than giving;
one should conduct oneself with impartiality—that is the way of the wise.
"Oh, how wonderful! May I alone be the one to give!"
May holy men and true persons associate with me;
like a rain cloud filling the lowlands,
may I satisfy all those who live as seekers of the spiritual life.
One whose facial expression brightens upon seeing a supplicant,
and who is joyful after giving, [is truly a giver].
Happy is that house for one who dwells therein,
where, upon seeing a beggar,
the expression of the face brightens with joy.
Having given, he is glad;
this is the perfection of sacrifice.
Even before giving, he is joyful.
One should gladden the mind while giving;
having given, one becomes joyful—
this is the perfection of sacrifice.
In the residence of Aṅkura, sixty thousand cartloads of food were constantly given.
For a person seeking merit,
there were three thousand cooks adorned with earrings of strung gems.
Sixty thousand men,
engaged in giving and sacrifice,
subsist upon that sprout.
Wearing earrings of supreme jewels,
young men were splitting firewood for the great almsgiving of Aṅkura.
Sixteen thousand women,
adorned with every ornament,
[attended] upon Aṅkura at his great almsgiving.
Sixteen thousand women, adorned with every ornament,
gathered together in groups.
At Aṅkura’s great almsgiving,
vessels of sour gruel were presented;
he gave much to many.
For a long time, the Kṣatriya served you,
honoring you with his own hands,
with due respect, and again and again.
For many months and fortnights,
and for seasons and years,
he bestowed a great gift.
For a long time, Aṅkura,
having thus given and sacrificed,
for a long time, Aṅkura.
Thus, having abandoned the human body,
he went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven after giving a spoonful of almsfood.
Indaka was the attendant of Anuruddha;
having cast off his human body,
he went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

And delightful tactile objects.
In terms of lifespan, fame,
complexion, and happiness;
By his sovereignty, Indaka outshines the sprout;
when the Buddha was among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, [he did so as well].
On the stone slab, the pale-yellow blanket,
at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree,
the Supreme Person dwelt.
Deities from ten world-systems, having assembled together,
pay homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Dwelling on the summit of the mountain,
no deity whatsoever surpasses the Perfectly Enlightened One in beauty.
Having surpassed all the gods,
the Fully Awakened One alone shines forth for twelve yojanas.
At that time, this sprout—
Indaka— shone forth not far from the Buddha.
Having observed both Aṅkura and Indaka, the Fully Enlightened One,
honoring them as worthy of offerings, said:
He spoke these words:
"A great gift was given by you,
Aṅkura, long ago."
"You are sitting too far away;
come near me. Thus was he urged by the one whose self was developed.
The sprout spoke thus:
"What have I to do with that gift,
which is empty of one worthy of offerings?"
This is that Indaka Yakkha,
who gives but a meager gift;
yet he outshines us.
“Just as the moon among the hosts of stars.
“Just as when seed is sown in great quantity in a field that is parched and barren;”
It does not yield abundant fruit,
nor does it satisfy the farmer;
even so is a gift that is merely abundant.
Established among those who are immoral,
it yields no abundant fruit,
nor does it satisfy the donor.
Just as even a small seed, when sown in a fertile field and provided with water properly, [thrives].
The fruit satisfies the farmer. Even so,
among those who are virtuous,
endowed with qualities, and such as these;
"Even a small deed performed becomes a merit of great fruit.
One should give a gift after having discerned [the recipient].
Where a gift given bears great fruit;
having given a gift with discernment,
the donors go to heaven.
Having discerned those worthy of offerings in this world of the living, who are praised by the Sugata—
gifts given to them yield great fruit.
"Seeds sown in a good field"—
thus ends the ninth *Aṅkurapeta-vatthu*.
